title: Jaap and the amrit bowl
hook: Jaap is one of the five banis recited over the iron bowl as amrit is prepared

segments.voice: Yesterday, sadaa, and your line, ever true, ever bliss. Sadaa ang sange, ever by your side. Today, where else Jaap is heard, besides the morning. Day three hundred fifty-seven, the end of a week.

A grandmother making soup. She doesn't just stir. She talks while she stirs: to the pot, to the kids in the doorway, sometimes under her breath to God. People who grew up in kitchens like that will swear the soup tasted different from anyone else's. Maybe it was the recipe. Maybe it was everything that got stirred in with it. There's a Sikh ceremony where that idea is taken with complete seriousness: words are stirred into water for a long time, and Sikhs say the water is never the same again. Today: Jaap and the amrit bowl.
screen: `A GRANDMOTHER STIRS AND TALKS.` → `THE SOUP TASTED DIFFERENT.` → `WORDS STIRRED INTO WATER.`

segments.voice: When a Sikh chooses to take amrit and join the Khalsa, the ceremony is called Amrit Sanchar. Five initiated Sikhs, the Panj Pyare, the five beloved ones, kneel around an iron bowl, a bata, filled with clean water. Into the water go patashe, small sugar sweets. Then the water is stirred with a khanda, a double-edged sword, while the Panj Pyare recite five banis, one after another. The first is Japji, Guru Nanak's. The second is Jaap Sahib. Then the Tav Prasad Savaiye, then Chaupai, then Anand Sahib. All of it, every stanza, is recited over the water as it's stirred. Think about what that means for Jaap. The salutations you've been learning, akaal, kripaal, aroop, ajooni, abhai, are recited into the water the new Khalsa drinks. The amrit is sprinkled on their eyes and hair, and they drink from the same bowl, whatever caste or family they came from. Tradition traces the ceremony to Vaisakhi in 1699, when the Tenth Guru first prepared amrit at Anandpur. A much-loved part of the story says the Guru's wife brought sugar sweets to the bowl, so that the iron and the steel would be joined by sweetness. Sources differ on the details, but Sikhs often say the point is clear: courage and kindness, stirred together. And this is where the week ends: the one-letter meter, abhai, fearlessness, the One in every land, death held in the One's hand, keeping the pace, the last stanza. And today, all of it, stirred in.
screen: `AMRIT SANCHAR: THE PANJ PYARE.` · `AN IRON BOWL, WATER, SUGAR, A KHANDA.` · `FIVE BANIS; JAAP IS THE SECOND.` · `SALUTATIONS STIRRED INTO WATER.` · then, large: `PRAYER STIRRED IN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stir a glass of water, reciting. This isn't amrit, and isn't meant to copy the ceremony. It's just a way to feel what words stirred into water might mean. Fill a glass. Stir it slowly with a spoon, round and round, and as you stir, say a line you know: namastvam akaale, namastvam kripaale. Then stop, set the spoon down, and drink the water slowly, noticing it go in. The bell holds the time.
Amrit. The nectar of immortality — the water stirred in the iron bowl while Jaap, the second of five banis, is recited over it for the Khalsa.
Your line: prayer stirred in. Today, while you make one drink or one meal, say something kind over it, and serve it to someone. Day three hundred fifty-seven. A week, done.

original.note: Gurmukhi: amrit, the nectar of immortality; the name of the water prepared for the Khalsa.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jaap is something Sikhs say alone in the morning.
what it means: it is also one of the five banis stirred into the amrit that initiates the Khalsa.
what a scholar hears: the Rehat Maryada lists the five banis of Amrit Sanchar; accounts differ on whether Mata Jito or Mata Sahib Kaur added the patashe.
